Getting started with cloudscape

Source: vignettes/cloudscape.Rmd
cloudscape.Rmd

The question this package is for

Most cloud software answers “which pixels are cloudy”. That is a means, not an end. The question behind it is usually “can I do my study here”, and answering that needs three things the mask alone does not give you: an unbiased spatial unit, an honest account of what scene metadata can and cannot tell you, and a translation from cloud statistics into the units your conclusions are stated in.

An unbiased spatial unit

Scene footprints are the wrong unit for statistics. A WRS-2 scene covers less ground area at high latitude, and neighbouring paths overlap more, so counting images per path/row conflates acquisition density with geometry. It also makes Landsat and Sentinel-2 incomparable, since their footprints differ.

g <- cl_grid(res = 100000)
box <- function(lat) cbind(c(0, 2, 2, 0, 0), c(lat, lat, lat + 2, lat + 2, lat))
nrow(cl_grid_index(box(50), g))   # cells covered at 50N
#> [1] 4
nrow(cl_grid_index(box(70), g))   # same 2x2 degrees at 70N
#> [1] 2

Every cell has the same true ground area, so counts are directly comparable across latitude and across sensors.

Units are enforced, not assumed 

cl_stats(1:2, "cloud_fraction", c(0.3, 1.4))
#> Error:
#> ! Metric 'cloud_fraction' has value 1.4 outside its permitted range [0, 1] (row 2).
s <- cl_stats(1:3, "n_scenes", c(20, 21, 22), period = "2023",
              denominator = "cell-year")
s$denominator
#> [1] "cell-year" "cell-year" "cell-year"

The denominator is part of the data. A total across ten years divided by ten is a mean per year; if it is labelled as a mean per scene, the numbers become physically impossible for the stated unit, and nothing in a plain data frame would catch that.

From cloud fraction to usable observations

Scene-level cloud cover is a scene average. Turning it into a per-pixel clear probability requires an assumption, and the naive one is optimistic:

d <- seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "5 days")
ts <- cl_simulate_series(d, p_cloud = 0.55, persistence = 0.35, seed = 2)
obs <- cl_obs(cell = 1, date = ts$date, cloud_fraction = ts$cloud_fraction,
              sensor = "sentinel-2-msi")
suppressMessages(head(cl_clear_prob(obs, "independent"), 3))
#> [1] 0.1008362 0.5124068 0.6671643
head(cl_clear_prob(obs, "clustered"), 3)
#> [1] 0.03796976 0.32011723 0.49134373

Cloud is clustered, so a scene reported as half cloudy is more often half covered by one deck than uniformly obscured. Tier-A results are upper bounds, and the package says so rather than leaving it implicit.

What actually breaks a time series

Not the mean. The longest stretch without a usable image.

cl_stats_wide(cl_gaps(obs, threshold = 0.2, critical = 30))
#>   cell period         sensor max_gap_days mean_gap_days n_clear_obs
#> 1    1   2023 sentinel-2-msi           50         14.56          24

Translating into days 

res <- lapply(c(0.3, 0.7, 0.9), function(p)
  cl_pheno_power(d, cloud_fraction = p, n_sim = 200, seed = 4)$summary)
do.call(rbind, res)[, c("n_usable_median", "sos_mae", "failure_rate")]
#>   n_usable_median sos_mae failure_rate
#> 1              51     0.9        0.000
#> 2              22     1.7        0.095
#> 3               7    12.3        0.635

The failure rate is often the more important column. In heavily clouded regions a study does not return a biased green-up date, it returns none at all.

Constellations change through time 

sy <- cl_synergy(c("landsat-8-9-oli", "sentinel-2-msi"),
                 "2014-01-01", "2025-12-31")
sy[sy$sensor == "COMBINED" & sy$period %in% c("2014", "2018", "2022", "2025"),
   c("period", "n_platforms", "effective_revisit_days")]
#>    period n_platforms effective_revisit_days
#> 25   2014           1              16.010959
#> 29   2018           3               3.812133
#> 33   2022           4               3.079031
#> 36   2025           5               2.354553

Sampling density is not stationary. Landsat 9 joined in late 2021 and Sentinel-2C in 2024, so a trend computed across such a period partly reflects acquisition capacity rather than the environment. Any long time-series analysis should account for this explicitly.
